name: Distribution Board
tagline: Where the supply splits into final circuits, each with its own protection and its own switch.
terminals: L-in and N-in from the meter and main earthing terminal
Circuit protective conductors to the earth bar
Neutral bar and earth bar — one way per circuit
Main earthing terminal and bonding connections
parts: Enclosure — metal on modern boards, with a hinged cover
Main switch — a double-pole isolator for the whole board
Circuit breakers, RCBOs and RCDs on a DIN rail
Busbar — the copper strip feeding the protective devices
safety: Live parts inside a consumer unit stay live with every circuit breaker off — only the main switch (or the cut-out fuse before it) makes the board safe. Only a competent person should remove a cover, and the supply must be isolated and proved dead first. Also note that a metal board and its circuits must be earthed and the bonding verified.

points.label: Enclosure
points.detail: Modern boards are metal, non-combustible and fitted with a hinged cover and blanks over every unused way. The blanking modules are not cosmetic: an open way leaves live busbar exposed to fingers and to anything dropped behind the cover.

points.label: Main switch
points.detail: A double-pole isolator that kills every circuit on the board. It does not protect anything — that is what the breakers do — and it does not isolate the incoming tails, which stay live from the cut-out.

points.label: Circuit breakers
points.detail: One protective device per final circuit, each sized to its cable. Type B for general purpose, Type C where the starting surge of a motor or transformer would nuisance-trip a B, and an RCBO where a single circuit needs its own 30 mA protection.

points.label: Busbar
points.detail: The copper comb that feeds live to every device on the rail. It is the reason the board is dangerous with all the breakers off: the busbar and the device line terminals are live whenever the main switch is on.

points.label: Neutral bar
points.detail: One way per circuit neutral, and the neutral must stay paired with its own circuit — mixing neutrals between circuits trips RCDs and can leave a conductor carrying current you do not expect after you have isolated.

points.label: Earth bar
points.detail: Circuit protective conductors and the main earthing terminal. Every CPC must land here; a CPC left floating in the board is a circuit with no fault path at all.

points.label: DIN rail
points.detail: The 35 mm rail every device clips onto. Devices must be seated and latched fully — a breaker clipped on by its top edge only can sit proud of the busbar and arc.

cutaway.alt: Cutaway of a distribution board showing the DIN rail, busbar, main switch, protective devices, neutral bar and earth bar

cutawayPoints.label: DIN rail
cutawayPoints.detail: The 35 mm top-hat rail every device clips onto. It carries no current — it sets the geometry. Get the rail straight and level and the busbar lines up with every line terminal in the board; get it wrong and you are fighting alignment on every way.

cutawayPoints.label: Busbar
cutawayPoints.detail: A comb of copper that feeds the line terminal of every device from one set of tails, so the supply does not have to be daisy-chained from breaker to breaker. The comb is cut for the board it ships with: mismatched devices leave teeth that do not line up with the terminals.

cutawayPoints.label: Main switch
cutawayPoints.detail: A double-pole isolator ahead of everything else, switching live and neutral so the entire board can be made dead with one movement — which is what makes safe isolation of a single circuit possible without killing the building.

cutawayPoints.label: Protective devices
cutawayPoints.detail: The MCBs, RCBOs and RCDs on the rail, one way per final circuit. Each carries its own overload and fault protection, and the arrangement is the design decision: an RCBO per circuit costs more but means one fault does not darken the whole house.

cutawayPoints.label: Neutral bar
cutawayPoints.detail: The common landing point for every circuit neutral, one way per circuit, with the incoming neutral tail on the same bar. A neutral that comes loose here does not just stop one circuit — on a shared-neutral arrangement it can put full voltage across equipment.

cutawayPoints.label: Earth bar
cutawayPoints.detail: Where every circuit CPC lands alongside the main earthing conductor and any bonding. On a TN-C-S supply this is the point at which the distributor combined earth and neutral becomes your installation earth, and the reason main bonding is sized the way it is.
